Reconstruct hourly temperatures from daily extremes

Source: R/hourly.R
hourly_temperatures.Rd

Builds an ordered, continuous hourly series (hours 0 to 23 of each day) from daily minimum and maximum temperatures. This is a modelling step with its own uncertainty: reconstructed hours are not observations.

Usage

hourly_temperatures(
  tmin,
  tmax,
  method = c("linvill", "sine"),
  latitude = NULL,
  doy = NULL,
  hour_tmin = 6,
  hour_tmax = 15,
  cyclic = FALSE,
  night = c("continuous", "chillr")
)

Arguments

tmin, tmax

Numeric vectors (or matrices with one row per series and one column per day) of daily extremes in degrees Celsius.

method

"linvill" or "sine".

latitude

Latitude in decimal degrees, required by "linvill". Scalar, or one value per row when tmin is a matrix.

doy

Day of the year of each day (required by "linvill").

hour_tmin, hour_tmax

Local times (hours) of the minimum and maximum for method = "sine".

cyclic

Treat the series as a closed annual cycle.

night

Pre-dawn formulation for "linvill": "continuous" (default) or "chillr" (see Methods).

Value

For vector input, a numeric vector of length 24 * length(tmin) ordered by day and hour. For matrix input, a matrix with one row per series and 24 * ncol(tmin) columns.

Methods

  • "linvill" (default): sine curve during daylight and logarithmic decay at night (Linvill 1990), with sunrise and sunset from daylength(). The minimum occurs at sunrise and daytime temperatures follow \(T_{min} + (T_{max} - T_{min}) \sin(\pi (h - h_{sr}) / (D + 4))\). Night temperatures decay from the sunset temperature to the minimum of the next day as \(\ln(h - h_{ss} + 1) / \ln(N + 1)\), where \(N\) is the night length. This is the formulation used by chillR::make_hourly_temps(); thermify uses the same \(+1\) offset before and after midnight, so the curve reaches exactly \(T_{min}\) at sunrise (chillR omits the offset in the pre-dawn denominator, giving values slightly below \(T_{min}\) just before sunrise and a small discontinuity at midnight). Set night = "chillr" to reproduce chillR exactly, for example when comparing with published chillR results.

  • "sine": continuous half-cosine segments joining \(T_{max,d-1} \to T_{min,d}\) (minimum at hour_tmin), \(T_{min,d} \to T_{max,d}\) (maximum at hour_tmax) and \(T_{max,d} \to T_{min,d+1}\). With hour_tmax - hour_tmin = 12 it is the symmetric sine; other timings give an asymmetric cycle. It does not need latitude and is consistent with the double sine degree-day method.

The extremes are reached exactly only at the modelled times; integer hours may therefore not include the exact daily minimum or maximum.

Boundaries

The first night needs the previous day's maximum and the last evening the next day's minimum. With cyclic = TRUE the series is treated as a closed climatological year (day 1 follows the last day). Otherwise the first day uses its own maximum and the last day its own minimum.

References

Linvill, D. E. (1990). Calculating chilling hours and chill units from daily maximum and minimum temperature observations. HortScience, 25(1), 14-16.

Luedeling, E. (2012). Climate change impacts on winter chill for temperate fruit and nut production: a review. Scientia Horticulturae, 144, 218-229.

Examples

h <- hourly_temperatures(c(2, 4), c(14, 16), latitude = -35.97,
                         doy = c(180, 181))
round(h, 1)
#>  [1]  4.2  3.8  3.4  3.1  2.8  2.5  2.3  2.0  4.4  7.0  9.3 11.3 12.8 13.7 14.0
#> [16] 13.7 12.8 11.2  9.4  8.4  7.6  7.0  6.5  6.1  5.7  5.4  5.1  4.9  4.6  4.4
#> [31]  4.2  4.0  6.4  9.0 11.3 13.3 14.8 15.7 16.0 15.7 14.8 13.1 10.9  9.5  8.6
#> [46]  7.8  7.2  6.7
hourly_temperatures(c(2, 4), c(14, 16), method = "sine")
